(a) RE-ENTRANCY: resolving a flight while holding the lock runs waiter continuations synchronously, and a continuation that reads state or requests another wake re-enters the same lock and DEADLOCKS the service. (b) UNBOUNDED HOLD: firing a magic packet, probing reachability or readiness, publishing to the broker and serving HTTP are all I/O, and performing any of them under the lock turns a bounded critical section into a lock wait as long as the slowest network operation - so one blocked probe stalls every joiner and every state read, including the health endpoint that would tell an operator why. THE RULE IS THEREFORE EXPLICIT: under the lock, and only under the lock, read the current state, join or start a flight, publish the terminal state, detach and remove the flight, and SNAPSHOT the waiter list. Release the lock. THEN notify the snapshotted waiters and perform every piece of I/O. Publication and removal still happen together so no arrival can interleave between them, which is what finding 3 of the prior round required and is preserved intact. THE FLIGHT OWNS THE DEADLINE: joiners neither extend, restart nor replace it, because a deadline any newcomer can refresh never expires under load, reintroducing the unbounded `waking` LLR-966 forbids; a late joiner inherits the remaining time. A flight resolves ONCE and every snapshotted waiter observes the same terminal outcome. On failure it resolves to `failed` and is cleared in the same critical section, so a subsequent request starts a NEW flight rather than joining a dead one.

Title: The policy reference is a document, and the check does not pretend otherwise
Detail: TAILSCALE POLICY LIVES SERVER-SIDE. The coordination service holds it, the daemon fetches it from there, and tailscaled never reads local disk for it - verified on the running hub 2026-09-18: nothing under /var/lib/tailscale, no unit file and no open file descriptor references the artifact. So a tracked policy file is a DOCUMENT TO PASTE INTO THE CONSOLE and nothing more, and this row previously claimed otherwise. An earlier version deployed it to the hub and had --check-only FAIL when it was absent or looked permissive. THAT CHECK WAS BACKWARDS AND IS REMOVED: it confirmed that a file this repo wrote said what this repo wrote in it, which is true whatever policy the tailnet is actually running - and it is false-green in the only case that matters, a wide-open policy applied in the console while the tracked file sits there looking correct. Verifying the policy in force needs a tailnet API key; that key can rewrite who reaches the entire LAN, and carrying one on the hub to catch the Owner's own console edits costs more than it saves under the standing threat model (ruled 2026-08-09, restated 2026-09-18). THE REFERENCE ALSO HAS TO BE RIGHT, and the first one was not, in two ways worth keeping: it placed an autogroup inside a `groups` entry, where members must be full email addresses, which the console rejects outright; and every rule targeted a tag while the hub authenticates AS A USER and carries no tag, so with deny-by-omission the policy accepted nothing and applying it would have cut off tunnel access to the hub. Both are asserted against the reference now. WHAT THE CHECK STILL DOES: it queries tailnet-lock state and WARNS when disabled, because that risk is a compromised coordinator or identity account - external, worth knowing, not worth refusing to converge over. The identity account's multi-factor property cannot be observed from this box and is not claimed; it is an operator attestation. AND THE URGENCY IS SCALED TO THE TAILNET: on a single-user tailnet the default policy means the Owner's own devices reach the Owner's own devices, which is fine. A policy starts mattering when a second person, a shared node or a tagged service appears.

Title: The fence is installed before the listeners and replays idempotently
Detail: The rules are installed by a unit ordered BEFORE and required by the owning service, so a failure to program either address family stops the listeners rather than leaving them unrestricted; this is the ordering the crossplay relay's own isolation unit already uses after its first version got it wrong and re-opened the window on every boot. The installer is IDEMPOTENT BY MARKER in both families: it removes its own prior rules before installing the current set, so a replay after a reboot converges rather than accumulating duplicates and a changed CIDR does not leave the older, wider rule behind. SCOPE, STATED PLAINLY. These ports are not forwarded at the router and this site has no inbound path from the internet at all, so this fence is a boundary against other devices on the home network, not against a determined attacker. Per the Owner's standing threat model it is NOT extended with reload hooks, watchdog timers or service-stop cascades to cover a hostile local actor flushing the ruleset - that scenario is explicitly out of scope, and the machinery it would require is not carried. Verification is that a connection from a source outside the LAN and tunnel ranges is refused on each documented TCP and UDP port.

Title: One owner starts the listeners
Detail: Both containers declare `restart: "no"`, so the container runtime never starts them on its own - not at boot, not after a daemon restart, not after a crash - and they are started only by homehub-rustdesk.service, which `Requires=` and is `After=` the isolation unit. A failure to program the fence therefore stops the listeners existing rather than losing a race to them. This is the ownership model the crossplay relay next door already uses, reused rather than reinvented. A deliberate manual compose start by the Owner is not defended against: it is the Owner's own machine and their own command, and per the standing threat model this row does not carry a mechanism to prevent it. The property that matters is that nothing starts these containers WITHOUT someone deciding to.

Title: The sleep inhibit needs an authoritative session signal, and it fails closed
Detail: LLR-969 requires the idle timer to be inhibited while an interactive remote-desktop session is attached and never said HOW that is known, which left the most damaging failure in this whole design undefined. THE SIGNAL IS AN EXPLICIT INTERFACE (IF-025) with a named source, a poll interval and a STALENESS BOUND: a reading older than that bound is not a reading. FAIL CLOSED MEANS ATTACHED. An absent, stale, malformed or unauthenticated session signal is treated as SESSION ATTACHED and the box is NOT slept. This direction is the whole point and the opposite of the usual instinct: the cost of a false 'attached' is that a machine stays awake and burns a few watts until the next reading; the cost of a false 'detached' is the machine sleeping under the Owner's hands mid-session, which SN-044 names as worse than never sleeping at all. A relay that reports a disconnected session as still attached therefore costs nothing this design cares about, while the reverse loses work. The inhibit is not the only condition - the idle period must also have elapsed with no local-model request - and an explicit operator override may force sleep, which is the one path permitted to ignore an attached session because a human is asserting the truth the signal cannot.

Title: One alias rule, imported by both sides of the privilege boundary
Detail: The root observer builds the document and the broker backend reads it, so a second spelling of the alias rule is how the renderer names a device the applier cannot find -- a refusal nobody can act on. STABILITY IS THE PROPERTY, not merely uniqueness: the renderer holds an alias between painting a row and the finger landing on it, so an alias carries forward from the previous publication and a device keeps it unless its own name changed. Ordering by address alone was tried and is stable only for a FIXED set -- a second device with the same name and a lower address took the bare alias and renamed the first. An alias freed by a rename is reserved while that device is still present, so it cannot be handed to another in the same pass; a DEPARTED device's alias is released, because nothing can be painted for a device the document no longer carries. A name that folds to nothing, or to something address-shaped -- which is what BlueZ calls an unresolved device -- gets a neutral alias instead. `classify` reads the panel-relative direction from the service UUIDs, and the two handsfree UUIDs are OPPOSITE roles: the unit is a headset (an output) and the gateway is a phone (an input).

Title: One device request per sequence, spooled for the root applier
Detail: A SPOOL DIRECTORY, not the one mailbox file the switch uses, and the difference is that switch verbs are idempotent and device verbs are not. With one file, two taps before the path unit fired left the first request overwritten, the applier advanced its high-water mark past BOTH sequences, and the completion check then reported the destroyed request as landed -- a revocation the person asked for, and was told had happened, that did not happen. Names are zero-padded so a lexical listing is a numeric ordering, and the writer's temporary is named so the drain skips it. The envelope is validated at the WRITING end as well as the reading end, because this file is the one thing that crosses from an unprivileged process into a root one and a boundary that validates only on the far side is a boundary that trusts the near one. The epoch is omitted rather than guessed when the applier's document cannot be read.

Title: The routed-device backend, layered over the switch backend
Detail: It WRAPS rather than replaces: the panel's own switch is a shipped control with its own applier, state file and reconciliation rules, and every non-device verb is delegated by ASKING the switch backend rather than by copying its list of methods. `inventory` never raises -- the broker treats anything but a list as an unsafe result -- so an unreadable document comes back EMPTY and every aliased verb refuses, which is the honest answer when the panel cannot see its own Bluetooth and is not the same as pretending the device is there. A document that is absent, the wrong version, malformed, from the FUTURE (which would never expire) or past its shelf life is "do not know". `request_landed` must be dispatched through `call`, because the broker probes for the attribute and then asks through the ordinary seam: without that it was never reached, and every device sequence was checked against the SWITCH applier's mark -- a coin toss between replaying a `forget` and dropping a `pair`. The minted sequence outranks both this process's last and the applier's persisted mark, because a broker restart resets the former and a backwards clock step then lands below the latter, silently.

Title: The root device applier: drain, perform, publish
CodeSymbol: wall-bluetooth-device.publish; wall-bluetooth-device.apply_request; wall-bluetooth-device.perform; wall-bluetooth-device.safe_name; wall-bluetooth-device.drain_lock; wall-bluetooth-device.inventory; wall-bluetooth-device.resolve; wall-bluetooth-device.pairing_block
Detail: The privileged half. It drains the spool in sequence order under a NON-BLOCKING lock, because the path unit and the observe timer are different units and systemd will run both -- two drains would perform one request twice. The mark and the file both move BEFORE the action, so a process that dies mid-pairing does not re-run it; the person taps again. The bound is a safety net and must not be a trap: a spool the bound or a failed unlink leaves behind is picked up by the observe timer within its period, rather than depending on whether a level-triggered path unit fires again for a directory that was already non-empty. `publish` is bounded end to end -- the listing and the last probe included -- and reports "do not know" rather than presenting the devices it managed to read as the whole list. `safe_name` substitutes any name containing a hardware address, which BlueZ produces for an unresolved device: without it the address crossed into the document AND the broker's validator then rejected the whole document, so one unresolved device cost every other device its row. The pairing WINDOW is not reimplemented here; `set_discoverable` calls the tool that already bounds it three ways over.

Title: Saving and restoring the panel player sign-in
CodeSymbol: wall-pandora-session.save; wall-pandora-session.restore; wall-pandora-session.status; wall-pandora-session._safe_members; wall-pandora-session.profile_locked; wall-pandora-session.auth_cookies
Detail: Only the credential-bearing files are carried; the caches are the bulk of the profile, carry nothing that authenticates, and are a liability beside a newer application. A save refuses when a keyring is installed, because the cookie key would then live somewhere the archive does not and the restore would produce a profile full of cookies nobody can read -- a silent failure that looks exactly like the problem it was meant to fix. The archive is operator-supplied input unpacked as root, so every member is checked and the whole restore is abandoned on any refusal: `str.lstrip` takes a SET OF CHARACTERS and turned `../../../etc/shadow` into `etc/shadow`, so the escaping-path check never saw the `..` it exists for. A restore refuses a profile a live browser holds, distinguishing a live holder from the stale lock a killed browser routinely leaves; refuses to replace an existing sign-in without an explicit flag, which is what makes running it from firstboot on every boot safe; and refuses an archive carrying no cookie store, which otherwise restored cleanly, left this panel's own cookies in place and reported success.

Title: A client identity that does not move with the build
Detail: The runtime's default client identity carries BOTH the application version and the runtime version, and the dependency is a floating range -- so a rebuild moves the string with no change in the repository and no note anywhere, under a session the provider fronts with bot detection. The fix is to look like an ORDINARY browser rather than to freeze a string: the two runtime-only tokens are dropped and the engine version is reduced to its major, which is what browsers themselves send. The result therefore changes only on an engine major -- a deliberate bump, indistinguishable from an ordinary browser update -- and no longer on an application release or a runtime patch. Nothing is invented: a runtime string this does not understand leaves the default in place, because a made-up platform string is a worse lie than an honest one. The cookie-encryption backend is NAMED rather than sniffed from the desktop, which closes the one mechanism by which installing an unrelated package silently destroys every stored cookie, and is also what makes the archive portable between boxes.

Title: One deployment is the guarantee, and it is arithmetic rather than a rule
Detail: The routing table shall carry exactly one entry, whose api_base is the single permitted environment reference for the dev PC. The property defended is that a request reaching this process can reach the dev PC or fail, with no third outcome, because there is nowhere else to go. The credential slot holds a declared placeholder written in the clear on purpose - the dev PC's server has no authentication of its own and the client still requires the header - and the test asserts that exact string so a real key cannot be parked there later.

Title: No fallback of any kind, and no database that could add one
Detail: No fallbacks, default_fallbacks, context_window_fallbacks or content_policy_fallbacks at any depth, and the model store disabled so the committed file is authoritative. Upstream's fallbacks are OPT-IN, so absence IS the mechanism - which is precisely why it needs a test, an absent key being the kind of thing added back while debugging. With the model store enabled, a deployment added through the admin interface would override the file and the file would still read as one model.

Title: The hold decision, as a pure function over the readiness document
Detail: Returns proceed, wake, wait, expired or no-oracle. Precedence is ordered: ready outranks the cap, because a box that became ready on the final poll should serve the request rather than be refused by a clock. An already-waking flight is joined rather than re-fired. An UP state still waits, because what is being waited for is the weights reaching VRAM and not the power state. An UNRECOGNISED state requests a wake rather than proceeding, so a new state name from a future readiness service is not read as fine by an old hook. Kept separate from the I/O for the same reason the wake service is split from its own HTTP layer: the interesting behaviour is provable by a table instead of by a box.

Title: The refusal must be retryable to the lane in front, and must not resemble a rate limit
Detail: The public lane classifies retryability by SUBSTRING-MATCHING the error text, so both refusal messages carry 503 and unavailable, and neither carries 429, quota or rate limit - those would also produce a fallback but would put the dev PC on a rate-limit cooldown for the offence of being asleep. A message outside the matcher list makes the public lane fail the whole request instead of substituting, and it presents as the gateway being down rather than as the dev PC being asleep. The two messages are distinct on purpose: one says the dev PC is not ready, the other says readiness could not be determined.

Title: An absent readiness oracle disables the hold explicitly and says so once
Detail: An empty readiness URL means no hold, which is the correct configuration while the wake path is unverified: a cold request then fails in seconds rather than waiting out the cap against a wake that does not work. It is announced once at startup rather than left to be discovered, because a hold that is silently absent and a hold that is silently ineffective look identical from the caller's side. Timing values are validated at startup: non-finite, negative and non-numeric are refused, a zero poll interval is refused, a zero cap is accepted and means ask-once-do-not-wait, and a probe timeout below the first-probe floor is refused because the first probe is floored so that a zero-budget cap still gets one honest look - a configured timeout under that floor would make the documented bound of cap plus one probe timeout false. The readiness address is the .1 of the pinned subnet written literally, not a host-gateway mapping, which resolves to the default bridge's gateway and would be rejected by this lane's own host fence.

Title: The wake unit is installed unconditionally and enabled only on the knob
Detail: Until 2026-09-19 nothing installed this unit at all: the payload was deployed and was unreachable from systemd, so the physical S3/S5 test could not be run without hand-writing a unit file on the box. Install is now unconditional and enable is gated on DEVPC_WAKE_ENABLED, so the test is one systemctl start away while the service still stays disabled across reboots. Enabling is REFUSED when neither a MAC nor an alternative wake command is configured, because a unit that enables and then crash-loops fills the journal and reddens the monitor three levels from the cause. The knob DISABLES rather than merely declining to enable, because firstboot re-runs and a box whose knob was true and is now false would otherwise stay enabled for ever.

Title: The egress fence is the boundary; the config file is not
Detail: MEASURED against the pinned digest, not inferred: the proxy registers 32 provider pass-through routes independently of model_list, and its Vertex handler forwards CALLER-SUPPLIED credentials when it holds none of its own, logging 'default_vertex_config not set, forwarding caller-provided headers'. A probe request with an x-goog-api-key header opened a connection to aiplatform.l.rep.googleapis.com:443. The credential can therefore arrive IN THE REQUEST, so its absence from the configuration was never a boundary. The boundary is below the application: the container takes a STATIC address on a PINNED subnet, and DOCKER-USER rules permit that address to reach the dev PC's inference port plus established return traffic and REJECT everything else. BOTH CHAINS ARE REQUIRED AND THE FIRST VERSION HAD ONLY ONE. DOCKER-USER carries the forwarded half. Packets addressed to the host's own bridge address are delivered locally and DOCKER-USER never sees them, so an INPUT half is also needed; the first version asserted that half was covered by the game fence, which covers a different subnet entirely - measured on the live box, INPUT held a reject for the game subnet and nothing for this lane, leaving SSH, cockpit and the DNS admin console reachable, the last of which can rewrite every name the household resolves. The INPUT half permits only the bridge gateway on the readiness port, is inserted below the mesh-tunnel jump and above every blanket accept - both constraints measured on the live chain, since appending would place it below an accept matching any source and inserting at the head would jump the tunnel admission - is inserted in reverse order so the rules emerge established, allow, deny, and verifies both that order and that no accept precedes its reject. The script refuses to program a partial rule set, refuses a hostname because iptables resolves a name once at program time and the rule then outlives the answer, reads every rule back, and verifies their ORDER - three correct rules in the wrong order are a fence that either kills the lane or opens it. The container carries restart:no and is started only by a unit that Requires= the fence unit, so the runtime can never bring it up unfenced; the fence unit is enabled unconditionally while the lane unit is enabled only on the knob, because a fence with no container is harmless and a container with no fence is the failure being prevented. allowed_routes in the proxy config removes the pass-through routes as DEFENCE IN DEPTH and is explicitly not the guarantee, being policy evaluated by the component it constrains. Verified on the running container: those routes answer 403 in user_api_key_auth before any handler and before any outbound attempt. The chain parser's column assumption is proved every run by counting the script's own just-inserted accept rules through the same expression and failing closed when it cannot find them, because a shifted column would make every ordering check pass vacuously. The deployed readiness url is validated against the host-directed allow rule at install time, since a file-level test can only see the example and a real environment naming the default bridge would be denied by this fence and reported for ever as an unreachable oracle. IPv6 is handled by verifying the network has none rather than by programming a rule for traffic that cannot exist, and the lane refuses to start if that premise ever breaks.

Title: Delivering the tracked stack tree to a running hub, and verifying it landed
Detail: THERE WAS NO LANE, AND THE ONE THAT LOOKED LIKE IT WAS FOR SOMETHING ELSE. /opt/homehub is a plain deployed tree that arrived from the autoinstall ISO, and stack/README.md's 'Enabling a service on a RUNNING box' is `$EDITOR .env` plus `docker compose up -d` - correct for the tier-2 catalog, whose services are a compose profile and an upstream image and need nothing new on disk, and wrong the moment a service ships files. Measured on the live hub 2026-09-19 the drift was never only the new lane: 14 tracked files absent and 15 stale, including docker-compose.yml with no litellm service and no llmprivate network, and autoinstall/firstboot.sh - so the idempotent re-run that is supposed to install units would have installed nothing new. THE SOURCE OF TRUTH IS A COMMIT, via `git archive`, never the working tree: a dirty tree is how half of someone else's change reaches a box, and this repo has already paid for working-tree-as-truth once. THREE RULES IT MAY NOT BREAK. (1) It never writes .env, *.creds or secrets/: the box's .env is the only copy of its live configuration and credentials, and .env.example beside it is a template of placeholders - but the TEMPLATE IS delivered, because it is how an operator learns a release needs a new knob. (2) It never deletes: files the repo does not track are left alone, which covers docker-compose.override.yml, llm-gateway.env, the deployed panel-access/app bundle and every __pycache__. (3) It preserves inodes - every file is placed with `cat staged > target`, because install, mv, cp and tar -x all unlink and recreate, which detaches a compose bind mount and leaves the container serving the old bytes through a reload that reports success. The litellm service bind-mounts two INDIVIDUAL FILES, so that is this lane's second delivery onwards, not a hypothetical. THE HUB/PANEL BOUNDARY IS BY USAGE, NOT BY NAME, and the names mislead in both directions: panel-audio/ is inert on the hub and excluded, while wall-shell/ is bind-mounted by caddy and served FROM the hub and must ship. DRY RUN IS THE DEFAULT and every delivered hash is read back FROM THE BOX afterwards, because a transfer returning zero means bytes moved, not that the right bytes are in the right place; a partial landing says so in those words and the tool is idempotent so the fix is to re-run it.

Title: `ready` is proved by a completion, not by a listing, and proving it never pins the card
Detail: `ready` MEANT `LISTED`, WHICH IS THE SAME LIE THIS SERVICE EXISTS TO PREVENT, ONE LAYER DOWN. devpc_wake.py opens by insisting that `up` is not `ready` - a woken box answers ICMP long before it can answer a prompt - and then decided readiness from a model LISTING. Both Ollama and llama-server list a model that is configured and NOT resident in VRAM, so a caller told `ready` still paid a full model load on its first request: `up` wearing `ready`'s name, and exactly the 'block on a completion and then blame the model' failure the file's own banner describes. A listing proves the model is CONFIGURED; only a completion proves it is LOADED. Readiness is therefore a ONE-TOKEN completion (max_tokens 1) against /v1/chat/completions, which is the smallest request that cannot be answered from a config file, and a 200 with no choices is rejected rather than trusted. THE COMPLETION IS NEVER FIRED BY THE POLLER, and that is not an optimisation. The service polls every DEVPC_WAKE_POLL_SECONDS to publish telemetry; a completion on that beat would hold the weights in VRAM permanently and defeat OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE, whose entire job is to hand the card back when the Owner wants to play a game - the watcher would silently prevent the thing it watches. So residency is verified only when a caller ASKS via /state, and the poller reuses the cached verdict. IT ALSO MUST NOT BLOCK THE ASK. The hold hook polls /state with a SHORT timeout while holding a request; a synchronous probe would time it out on a cold load, which the hook reads as no-oracle and REFUSES on, turning a sleeping box into a hard failure. The probe runs on a background thread, single-flight, and the ask returns immediately saying it is verifying; the next poll sees `ready` once the weights are genuinely there, which is the SR-044 hold falling out of not blocking. The verdict expires after DEVPC_READY_TTL_SECONDS so a model the keep-alive has evicted stops being advertised, and a refusal or timeout neither extends nor poisons the cache. The cheap listing is KEPT as a pre-filter, because it distinguishes 'this box serves a different model' - a configuration fault worth naming instantly - from 'the right model is there but cold', which is worth waiting out.

Title: The previous boot is classified into one of five classes, bound to its boot id
Detail: Order is the design's table with one override: a watchdog bootstatus carrying WDIOF_CARDRESET (0x20, decimal in sysfs) wins even over a stamp, because a late-shutdown hang reset by L4 is a watchdog reset when the firmware says so. Otherwise a stamp that names the previous boot is clean, or recovery when it carries an intent; a new pstore record is panic; anything else is unexplained. The previous boot id is the last-boot record this classifier writes every boot - NOT journalctl --list-boots, which the design names: the journal is what a hard reset is most likely to leave dirty and it is bounded by retention, so it is used only as a fallback when a stamp exists and no record does. With neither, the boot is 'first' and is not counted, so installing the capability does not charge the brake. pstore records are compared against a seen-list because systemd-pstore moves them at boot; the unit runs after systemd-pstore and systemd-modules-load.

Title: Accounting commits are atomic and an uncommitted boot is report-only
Detail: Every durable write is temp file, fsync, rename, fsync of the directory; a failure removes the temp file and leaves the target as it was. boots.log is appended by rewriting the whole bounded file through that path, because an O_APPEND write can tear across a reset. The commit is boots.log, then the proof latch, the pstore seen-list and last-boot, then the stamp's deletion; any OSError makes the boot uncommitted, boot.json (tmpfs, always written) says so, kernel.panic is 0, and the supervisor reads it at startup and runs report-only, so an unwritable disk cannot bypass the brake. A second run within one boot appends nothing and only recomputes.

Title: The clean-shutdown stamp is written after Docker stops and carries the tmpfs intent
Detail: The stamp unit does nothing at start; its ExecStop writes {boot_id, utc, t, intent}. ORDERING DEVIATES FROM THE DESIGN TEXT, deliberately: the design writes After=docker.service and states the goal 'stops after Docker', but systemd stops units in the reverse of their start order, so After=docker would stop the stamp BEFORE Docker and a hung Docker stop would hide behind an already-written stamp. The unit therefore has Before=docker.service shutdown.target umount.target, After=local-fs.target, RequiresMountsFor= its paths, DefaultDependencies=no and Conflicts=shutdown.target. The intent is written by the supervisor to /run at request time, where a slow disk cannot block it, and rides to disk here.

Title: The brake, D10's counting policy and kernel.panic
Detail: Counted classes are recovery, watchdog, panic, plus unexplained unless the selected reset device is proven (LLR-1017). The brake engages when HUB_WD_MAX_RECOVERY_BOOTS counted boots fall inside one 24 h window and clears only when 24 h pass with no counted boot - a fourth counted boot 23 h after the third keeps it on - or after a brake-reset entry, which discards everything before it. The proof is written per device identity the first time that device reports CARDRESET and is never written on belief; counting is recomputed from stored classes, so it applies retroactively. kernel.panic is 10 only when the knob is on, the tier is full, the boot committed and the brake is off; otherwise 0.

Title: Victim choice, kill, confirmation, Docker reconciliation and quarantine
CodeSymbol: recovery_common.scan_container_scopes; recovery_common.read_inventory; recovery_common.choose_victim; recoveryd.decide_quarantine; Supervisor._kill; Supervisor._check_confirmations; Supervisor._reconcile; homehub-recovery.cmd_release
Detail: Candidates are docker-<64 hex>.scope cgroups under system.slice and homehub.slice up to two levels (the backup's slice included), with memory.current; host cgroups are never read as candidates. Identity comes from Docker's config.v2.json and hostconfig.json, refreshed every 30 s on a telemetry thread because it is disk I/O; an id missing from that inventory is skipped, since it could be a protected container recreated since. The largest identified container being protected is recorded as would-have-killed. The kill writes 1 to cgroup.kill; populated 0 within 10 s confirms it, otherwise kill-did-not-take is recorded and the episode continues. Reconciliation runs docker inspect (20 s) and, for a container reported running whose cgroup is empty, docker rm -f for restart policy no or empty, docker restart otherwise; an unanswered Docker is retried every 60 s up to ten times and nothing waits on it. Quarantine is decided by compose service (else name): the third selection within an hour still writes cgroup.kill so relief does not wait on Docker, spends no budget, and queues docker update --restart=no plus docker stop; the CLI's release restores the recorded policy and starts the container.

Title: The memory state machine runs on monotonic time and counts only measured samples
Detail: States NORMAL, PRESSURED, COOLDOWN. A measured pressured sample in NORMAL opens an episode at t0. A kill needs now-t0 >= HUB_WD_KILL_SECONDS, budget left, at least half the samples the window could hold, and the pressured share of the window's measured samples at or above HUB_WD_KILL_MEASURED_PCT. The half-full floor is an implementation constant the design does not state: without it two pressured samples either side of a long gap read as 100 % pressured. Unreadable PSI adds no sample. A gap (> 15 s between iterations) is recorded and only lets monotonic time pass inside an open episode. Clear is 60 s of measured calm with at least three samples; a kill never resets t0, only a clear does; the reboot decision fires once per episode at HUB_WD_REBOOT_SECONDS from t0. The wall clock is never consulted; BOOTTIME minus MONOTONIC growing by more than 5 s resets the episode and keeps the kill budget.

Title: One action thread with non-droppable deduplicated queues; telemetry may block for ever
Detail: Every main-thread queue operation is a single deque append: no lock a blocked worker could hold. Actions have one deque per kind, served in the order reboot, restart_ssh, quarantine, reconcile, and the main thread deduplicates by (kind, key) in flight; a reboot is never re-queued once requested, whatever its result. Telemetry is one deque of 256 that drops its oldest item and counts the drop; two daemon threads serve it and may block indefinitely in fsync or on journald. Workers are started with a 256 KiB stack before mlockall and drop themselves to SCHED_OTHER; a worker that cannot is a setup failure. The SIGTERM path gives telemetry one second and then exits with os._exit so a blocked daemon thread cannot hold the interpreter.

Title: Execution envelope, modes and knob validation
CodeSymbol: recovery_common.parse_config; recovery_common.Config; homehub-recovery.cmd_check_config; Supervisor.setup; Supervisor.safe_tick; homehub-recoveryd.service
Detail: The unit sets OOMScoreAdjust=-1000, SCHED_RR priority 1 with ResetOnFork, LimitRTTIME=2s:4s, LimitMEMLOCK=128M, MemoryMax=128M, MemoryMin=64M, Restart=no, KillMode=mixed. Setup reads boot.json, starts the workers, preallocates the ring and calls mlockall(MCL_CURRENT|MCL_FUTURE) through libc, and only then opens the device; any failure leaves it closed and the mode report-only with the reason in status.json. Modes: full (tier full, accounted, unbraked), contain (tier contain), braked (as contain, by the brake), report-only (records would-have for every action). A MemoryError in a tick stops petting and the process stays alive, so a restarted instance cannot re-arm. Knobs are validated in one place: empty means default; enums, ranges, the reboot exceeding the kill window, container names and earlyoom pairs with KILL <= TERM are checked and a violation names its knob. HUB_WD_TIERS and HUB_WD_RESET_DEVICE are additions to the design's knob table, both defaulting to the cautious value, so P3 can ship without P4.

Title: SIGTERM hands the device to the shutdown; only an explicit disarm closes it

Detail: WDIOC_KEEPALIVE 0x80045705 and WDIOC_SETTIMEOUT 0xC0045706, checked against linux/watchdog.h. SIGTERM and SIGINT are blocked before any thread exists and collected by sigtimedwait in the main loop. SIGTERM NEVER DISARMS (amended after review C2): the device timeout becomes HUB_WD_SHUTDOWN_SECONDS, it is petted once and closed without 'V'. A disarm is SIGUSR1: the disarm file is read and deleted, and authorises a disarm only when its two fields equal this boot id and INVOCATION_ID; the verified protocol is LLR-1010. A reboot request writes the intent to /run, queues systemctl reboot (30 s), and if no SIGTERM arrives within 120 s petting stops regardless of the action thread.

Title: One hub-pressure record every 30 s, protected items in full
Detail: One compact JSON line per run on stdout, SyslogIdentifier hub-pressure: memory/io/cpu some and full avg10/avg60; MemTotal, MemAvailable, SwapTotal, SwapFree; every container scope by name, largest first, tagged when it is in the backup slice; every protected container whatever its size; ssh, tailscaled and homehub-recoveryd as cgroup memory.current plus summed VmRSS of cgroup.procs; the top five processes by VmRSS; the count and first twenty D-state tasks. Timer OnUnitActiveSec=30s with AccuracySec=1s; the service is bounded to 25 s and 64M.

Title: The backup's own slice, its exact peak, its opt-in limit and the staging refusal

The slice is a static unit with MemoryAccounting=yes, enabled so it stays active. The wrapper reads the slice's ControlGroup from systemd (or FILEBACKUP_SLICE_CGROUP) and logs memory.peak after the backup and after the verify; an unreadable slice is logged and never fails the run. Before the container, a Temp directory under the change root refuses the run with 'LIBRARY BACKUP REFUSED: staging needs recovery (interrupted by recovery event <id>)', where id is the newest event file newer than Temp that contains interrupts_backup true, else the newest newer one, else 'none recorded'; Temp is not touched. That refusal is to be removed when FileBackup recovers killed staging itself (D8).

Title: setup-recovery.sh converges the opt-in half on or off

Detail: Knobs are read with the same _env_val idiom as firstboot and validated by the CLI's check-config (exit 2, nothing changed). ON writes recovery.env, /etc/default/earlyoom (-m TERM,KILL -s TERM,KILL -r 3600) and the tailscaled OOMScoreAdjust=-1000 drop-in, enables and restarts earlyoom when installed and says so when it is not, re-runs the classifier and restarts the supervisor. The full tier chooses wdat_wdt (only with an ACPI WDAT table), then iTCO_wdt, then softdog, unloading a module that produced no watchdog0, persists it in modules-load.d and installs RebootWatchdogSec/WatchdogDevice, re-executing PID 1 only when that drop-in changed. OFF runs the verified disarm (LLR-1010) first and exits 1 having changed nothing if it cannot be proven, then disables it, removes the three drop-ins and earlyoom's enablement, writes enabled=false and sets kernel.panic=0. No ssh.service drop-in is ever written.

Title: sshd is probed by its banner and restarted only while memory is normal
Detail: Every 60 s, and only in NORMAL, the main thread connects to 127.0.0.1:22 and requires 'SSH-' within 4 s: with ssh.socket the kernel completes the handshake even when sshd is wedged, so only the banner proves sshd. HUB_WD_SSH_FAILS consecutive failures queue one deduplicated systemctl restart ssh (60 s) and reset the count; in report-only it is recorded as would-have.

Title: Every action leaves a kmsg line now and an evidence file when the disk allows
Detail: Actions write '<5>homehub-recoveryd: <action> k=v ...' to /dev/kmsg from the main thread through a non-blocking descriptor, and queue an evidence item carrying the ring of the last 48 samples already in memory; telemetry writes it atomically to events/<UTC>-<boot8>-<action>.json. A kill or reboot that interrupts the backup carries interrupts_backup true. No docker ps and no global sync anywhere. Routine events go to the journal only.

Title: Accounting that decides the brake is read strictly and fails closed
Detail: Review C4. read_boots_log_strict returns [] only when boots.log does not exist; any other OSError, a line that is not JSON, or a line that is not an object with a numeric t raises AccountingError. The classifier then commits nothing (not even on a same-boot re-run), records committed=false, takes the brake as ON with counted_recent -1, writes kernel.panic 0, and the supervisor starts report-only. parse_boots_log, which skips bad lines, is kept for the CLI's display only. evaluate_brake is the one place that reads the log to decide, shared by the classifier and the running supervisor (LLR-1011).

Title: The reset device is stopped only verifiably, and never abandoned
CodeSymbol: Supervisor._arm; Supervisor._timeout_error; Supervisor._release_device_verified; Supervisor.on_disarm_request; Supervisor._disarm_orphan_at_start; homehub-recovery.cmd_disarm; homehub-recovery._orphan_disarm; setup-recovery.sh disarm_first
Detail: Reviews C1, C2, C3. ARMING: HUB_WD_HW_TIMEOUT and HUB_WD_SHUTDOWN_SECONDS are checked against sysfs min_timeout and max_timeout (0 = no upper bound) BEFORE the device is opened, because opening starts it; an unreadable range refuses. A failure after open keeps the descriptor, disarms and verifies, and goes report-only only on verified inactive; otherwise the device is held and petted and status is red with arm_error. RELEASE: WDIOC_SETOPTIONS(WDIOS_DISABLECARD) 0x80045704, then 'V' and close, then sysfs state must read inactive (or the device be absent); otherwise it is reopened and petted. DISARM: the CLI writes the boot+invocation authorisation, sends SIGUSR1, waits for an acknowledgement naming both, reads sysfs itself, and only then stops the unit and reads sysfs again; anything less exits 1 with the supervisor running. An active device with no supervisor is opened, magic-closed and verified when nowayout is 0. SETUP decides first and, if anything changes, runs that disarm BEFORE writing a file and then STARTS (not restarts) the replacement; an unchanged re-run leaves the running supervisor alone. A supervisor that will not arm, finding the device active at start (a predecessor's hand-off), takes it over and stops it, or holds and pets it. reset-brake replaces through the disarm. The non-magic hand-off is used only on SIGTERM.

Title: The running supervisor re-evaluates the brake every 10 minutes
Detail: Review C9. Every BRAKE_CHECK_SECONDS (600) in full, braked or contain mode the main thread queues a brake-check; a telemetry thread reads the accounting through evaluate_brake (disk I/O stays off the main thread) and posts the verdict; an AccountingError posts braked. Engaging: verified release of the device (a device that will not stop is kept and petted), mode braked, kernel.panic 0. Clearing: in the full tier re-arm only through _arm and its range validation, a refusal leaving it braked; then mode full and kernel.panic 10; in contain, mode contain. The tmpfs boot.json is updated to match. A telemetry thread blocked for ever stops the re-evaluation and leaves the current mode, which is recorded as a limit.

Title: A container with unreadable metadata has no identity and is never chosen
Detail: Review C5. An inventory entry needs a parseable config.v2.json with a non-empty string Name and a Config object (Labels an object if present) and a parseable hostconfig.json. Missing, corrupt or unreadable files leave the container out of the inventory, so choose_victim treats it as unidentified and skips it; a blank-name ContainerInfo, which no protect entry can match, is never created.

Title: Quarantine state is written by one writer at a time, newest snapshot winning
Detail: Review C6. The main thread queues numbered snapshots; a telemetry thread writes one under a lock that only telemetry threads take, and drops any snapshot older than the last written. atomic_write's temp file is path.tmp.<pid>.<thread>.<counter>, opened O_EXCL, so concurrent writers never share or truncate one.

Title: The running tailscaled is protected before earlyoom starts
Detail: Review C7. systemd applies OOMScoreAdjust at spawn, so the drop-in alone leaves a running tailscaled at its old score. Setup reads its MainPID, writes -1000 to /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj and reads it back; only then is earlyoom enabled and started. If a running tailscaled cannot be protected (write refused or value not kept), earlyoom is not started and setup says so; with no tailscaled running the drop-in covers its next start.

Title: An unmeasured sample or a gap breaks the calm streak
Detail: Review C8. Clearing needs CLEAR_SECONDS of consecutive MEASURED calm: an iteration with unreadable PSI, or one that arrives as a gap, resets the streak, so a few seconds of calm followed by an unmeasured stretch cannot close an episode and discard its reboot clock.

Title: A quarantined service is kept stopped after every boot's compose up
Detail: Review 2026-10-10. docker update --restart=no holds against dockerd but not against firstboot's docker compose up -d, which starts every stopped service whatever its policy. The up's exit status is captured rather than left to set -e, so the next command, homehub-recovery enforce-quarantine, runs even when the up failed partway; the up's failure is then propagated as set -e would have. Quarantined services are not left out of the up: the bare up's service set comes from the active profiles, and a depends_on would start the service anyway. The enforcement reads only quarantine.json (so it holds with the supervisor off). The supervisor records the victim's compose project and service with its full id; a compose victim resolves to its current container by BOTH the com.docker.compose.project and com.docker.compose.service labels, with the recorded id as the fallback, and a victim with no recorded project is its recorded id only - so a same-named service of another project is never touched. Each target gets docker update --restart=no and docker stop. A failed stop exits 1 and firstboot logs it; it never fails the boot. release resolves the container the same way, so a service the boot recreated under a new id is the one released; released entries leave the file and are never stopped again. Known limit: the service runs for the seconds between the up and the enforcement.

Title: D10's proof is bound to the reset device that gave it
Detail: Review 2026-10-10. bootstatus-proven holds the kernel identities (/sys/class/watchdog/<dev>/identity) of every device that has reported WDIOF_CARDRESET; a device with no readable identity proves nothing, and the old unbound plain-text latch proves nothing. Unexplained boots stop counting only while the device recovery.env's HUB_WD_DEVICE selects has one of those identities; no selected device (contain tier, none, off) or a different one (a fall-back to softdog) counts them again, retroactively within the 24 h window. The boot classifier and the supervisor's periodic re-evaluation decide through the same function.

The template carries no User=, ReadWritePaths= or CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR; the per-instance drop-in does: account 1 gets ~/.claude and ~/.claude.json (the old unit's paths), account 2 gets ~/.claude-2 and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR only. claude2 and gemini units exist only when named in AI_USAGE_SOURCES and are removed when dropped. A bucket with no modelId or no numeric fraction is skipped as the CLI skips it; any other fault (fraction outside 0..1, unusable window, a configured model with no bucket) refuses the whole reading because the answer is a minimum. The label names the model set, falling back to a count and never to a truncated list.
